relevant_group_routes.relationship: Labroussian economic and social history at Laval
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Savard (1974) says Ouellet owed a debt to Labrousse and Chaunu; Robert Mandrou prefaced Ouellet’s 1966 book (review heading). Dechêne trained in France in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert before her Paris doctorate (1973), published as Habitants et marchands (1974) (Charron, Dictionnaire universel des créatrices; formal supervision not asserted). Linteau (1983) says social history began in Quebec in the 1960s under Annales influence but that his generation was shaped more by French and Quebec sociologists and American historians. Specific contributions to the Laval and New France strands, not an Annales origin for Quebec historiography.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The modernist generation adopts social history
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Linteau (1983) describes his cohort adopting social history and serial sources (censuses, civil registers), becoming more quantitative, and widening the subject from French Canadians to Quebec’s whole population. Self-description of one generation.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The metropolis–hinterland approach, taken up by Canadian urban historians in the 1970s and then contested by them (1954–85)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own statements. The 1954 article proposes the metropolis and its hinterland as a field of study, including 'social and cultural associations' as well as economic ties (pp. 17–18), and names Masters's The Rise of Toronto as the closest application (p. 17). In 1981 he writes that 'urban history' grew within regional writing because cities 'are also centres that focus and structure regions or sub-regions about them. The interplay of city and region thus demands and has received attention', and that he had 'always sought to emphasize the reciprocal and complementary nature of the relations between the great city and the territory it dominates' (Manitoba History no. 1, web text). Davis (1985) lists his urban-history articles: 'Urban Development in Canada', Urban History Review 1 (1974), and 'Metropolis and Region', Urban History Review 3 (1979) (nn. 6, 11; unread). In-period reception, from Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), read in full: 'In the 1970s metropolitanism helped preside over the birth of a new sub-discipline, urban history', and according to Artibise and Linteau (1984) the articles by Careless on metropolis and region 'marked, in some ways at least, the self-conscious beginning of urban history' in Canada (p. 96; a quoted-in witness); urban historians 'have remained the most faithful to the metropolitan concept of J.M.S. Careless, the godfather of their subdiscipline' (p. 96); Gilbert Stelter called the metropolitan thesis in 1977 'the most significant approach to Canadian urban history' (p. 96, quoted). A contribution, contested within the field: Davis argues that 'there is no single metropolitan thesis' (p. 107), that Careless's approach 'has fallen into desuetude in historical circles' (p. 103), that Artibise found the metropolis/hinterland concept 'not really a theory that explain[ed] Canadian urban development' (p. 103, quoted), and that urban historians 'might do better by abandoning the metropolitan approach altogether' (abstract, p. 95). Davis also records Careless's own reserve: he would 'disclaim and deny such a metropolitan “thesis”' (p. 96, quoting 1973). This is a Canadian contribution; it does not claim that Dyos's or US urban history drew on Careless. edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition, critique) stays: it records the field's rejection of metropolitanism, this edge the field's use of it.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Metropolis and hinterland in Canadian urban history, 1954–85

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Ouellet's critiques of two interpretations: the Montreal school's Conquest thesis (Séguin's 'décapitation' of a national bourgeoisie, taken up by Brunet), with the habitant's trauma placed in the failing agrarian system rather than the Conquest (1962–85); and parts of the post-1960 generation's economic history, organised in his reading, in 'une grande partie' of it, around French-Canadian inferiority and the independence movement, whose revisions of Séguin's thesis Linteau, Robert and Normand Séguin followed (1985)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The Montreal school. His own texts. 1962 (with Hamelin, read): French-Canadian historiography reflects 'les réactions émotives des classes dirigeantes canadiennes-françaises', and its simplifications result 'à la fois du mépris de l'économique et de l'idéalisation du fait politique' (p. 32; no historian is named). 1976 (read): 'Si notre « habitant » a subi un traumatisme, ce n'est pas au moment de la conquête mais au moment où le système agricole traditionnel ne peut plus fonctionner comme autrefois' (p. 116). 1985 (read): 'pour Maurice Séguin, théoricien de l'École néo-nationaliste', the leadership of New France belonged to the bourgeoisie, 'de sorte que la décapitation s'était exercée sur l'élite nationale elle-même' (p. 18); 'Cette thèse avait été épousée par Michel Brunet dès les années 1950'; in the 1970s 'la thèse de la dégradation de la bourgeoisie avait besoin d'être dédramatisée', and 'Ces retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin furent faites par Gilles Paquet et Jean-Pierre Wallot, en particulier' (p. 19); at the core of the crisis controversy stood 'la thèse néo-nationaliste enrichie de l'idée de modernité' (p. 25). In 1984 (recorded by the 1.136 Creighton packet, not re-read here) he asked whether the scheme of Séguin, Frégault and Brunet was 'bien différent' from Creighton's post-Conquest 'société semi-féodale décadente' (p. 227). In-period Montreal reader: Tousignant (1980) on 'la profondeur du fossé qui séparait Fernand Ouellet de l'école néo-nationaliste de l'Université de Montréal et de son maître à penser, le professeur Maurice Séguin' (p. 419), and, as Tousignant reports, Ouellet had 'raillé le schéma d'interprétation freudien de l'école néo-nationaliste de Montréal à propos du «choc» de la Conquête' (p. 423); the text Tousignant refers to was not identified or read. Séguin has no entry, so the edge targets the montreal_school strand. The modernists. His own text, 1985 (read for pp. 11–29 and the pages named): the dominant preoccupation of most of those who built the new economic history 'était par trop centrée sur la situation précaire des Canadiens français en Amérique du Nord', a feeling 'pas étranger à la montée du mouvement indépendantiste québécois'; the themes of dependence, of Quebec's lag behind Ontario and of francophone inferiority 'imprègnent d'une façon ou d'une autre une grande partie de cette historiographie', and 'ces préoccupations ont entraîné les historiens à négliger des secteurs entiers de l'histoire économique et, par conséquent, à se fermer nombre de voies d'accès à une explication du social' (p. 18); after Paquet and Wallot's 'retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin' (p. 19), 'On peut en dire presque autant des études de Jean-Claude Robert, de Paul-André Linteau et même de Normand Séguin sur le caractère dynamique de la bourgeoisie foncière rurale et urbaine' (pp. 19–20). The same 1985 survey also credits the period with the emergence of a more scientific social history; the passages above are its critical ones, and their limits ('une grande partie', 'presque autant') are kept. In-period reader: Rudin's characterisation, not Ouellet's: Rudin (1995, ¶9–10) describes Ouellet's 1985 and 1988 texts as 'une condamnation virulente de l'historiographie québécoise récente' that associates the revisionists with the 'mouvement indépendantiste des années 1970'; Rudin himself (1995b, p. 66) places Ouellet's emphasis on 'mentalités' beside his own. Limits: the 1988 English version and the 1991 essays Rudin also cites are unread; Ouellet's survey is a long review of the field, and the critical passages read are those quoted. One arrow carries both because they share endpoints and type; the strands are montreal_school and modernist_synthesis.
